planting.note: Grow in a full-sun xeriscape bed or large container in fast-draining, mineral-rich cactus mix; this fast-growing columnar species tolerates light frost far better than most Echinopsis once established.

directions: Native to the Andean foothills of Ecuador and Peru, San Pedro cactus forms an upright, blue-green, multi-ribbed column that branches from the base with age into a candelabra-like clump. Large, sweetly fragrant, funnel-shaped white flowers open at night in summer and typically last only into the following morning. Water deeply but infrequently, letting the soil dry completely between waterings, and reduce watering further through cool winter months. Rooted stem cuttings callus for a week or two before potting into gritty, fast-draining soil to propagate new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Site in full sun in a xeriscape bed or large container with sharply draining cactus mix; golden spines color best under strong, direct light.

directions: Native to arid scrub in Argentina, this clustering columnar cactus is prized for its dense covering of bright golden-yellow spines along ribbed, blue-green stems, forming thickets of upright to leaning columns over time. Large, fragrant, white to pale yellow trumpet flowers open at night in late spring and summer and are pollinated by moths and bats in habitat. Water only when the soil has dried out fully, withhold water almost entirely through winter, and detach rooted basal offsets to start new plants. It tolerates brief dips below freezing better than many columnar cacti once mature.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect to direct light in a shallow pot with fast-draining cactus mix; the twisted spines are most attractive when the plant receives strong light.

directions: Native to Queretaro, Mexico, bird's nest cactus forms pale yellow-green globose stems covered in long, pliable, yellowish spines that curve and interlace over the surface like a woven basket. Small, star-shaped, cream to pale yellow flowers with a light honey fragrance appear scattered across the crown in spring, followed by slender pink-red fruit. It offsets readily from the base to form a tidy mounding cluster, making it an easy, fast-multiplying houseplant. Water only when the soil is fully dry and divide rooted offsets to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in a shallow container or rock garden pocket in bright light with gritty, fast-draining cactus mix; dense spination develops best under strong, direct sun.

directions: Native to the Sierra Madre Oriental of Tamaulipas, Mexico, this small globose cactus is densely clothed in fine, soft white to cream spines that give each head a plush, cushion-like appearance. Delicate pale pink flowers with darker pink midribs ring the crown in spring, followed by small pink fruit. It offsets readily from the base with age, forming a tight, multi-headed cluster prized by collectors. Water only when the soil is fully dry and separate rooted offsets to propagate new plants.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Site in full sun to light shade in a xeriscape bed or container with sharply draining cactus mix; this species tolerates cooler, drier winters better than many soft-bodied mammillarias.

directions: Native to the high central plateau of Mexico, this variable species bears large, prominent tubercles on a flattened, dull green stem that slowly clumps into a broad mound many inches across as older heads produce new offsets. Cream to pale yellow flowers with a reddish-brown midstripe open in a ring around the crown in spring, followed by red club-shaped fruit later in the season. It is among the most cold-tolerant mammillarias and handles brief winter chill better than most in its genus. Water only when the soil is fully dry and separate rooted offsets from the mound to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow in a shallow pot or rock garden pocket in bright light with fast-draining cactus mix; a distinct cool, dry winter rest encourages the heaviest spring flowering.

directions: Native to the highlands of Oaxaca and Puebla, Mexico, this cylindrical cactus is covered in short white radial spines and darker, hooked central spines set against soft green skin. Its main draw is the striking ring of bright magenta-pink flowers that wreathes the crown in spring, standing out sharply against the pale spination. It offsets slowly from the base over time, eventually forming a small cluster of heads. Water only when the soil is fully dry, keep nearly dry through winter, and separate rooted offsets to propagate.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
